```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
import {selectControl, loadWeekData, issueTargets, mmeSkillByLead, mmeSkillMaps, mmePatterns, mmeForecastMaps, mmeScoresByLead, mmeFlexible} from "../assets/leads/leads.js"
mme = loadWeekData("../assets/seasonal-mme-2023/")
geo = ({indonesia: await FileAttachment("../data/boundaries/indonesia.geojson").json(),
  provinces: await FileAttachment("../data/boundaries/provinces.geojson").json(),
  neighbours: await FileAttachment("../data/boundaries/neighbours.geojson").json()})
leadChoices = mme.targets.map(t => [String(t.lead), `Lead ${t.lead}: ${t.label}`])
modelChoices = mme.models.map(m => [m, m === "MME" ? "MME (the ensemble)" : m])
memberChoices = modelChoices.filter(([m]) => m !== "MME")
```

::: {.eyebrow}
Template · Seasonal · Multi-model ensemble · Full Indonesia
:::

The [single-model seasonal case](seasonal-leads-2023.qmd) asked what one CFSv2 run
could say about the next six seasons. This case asks the same question of **every
seasonal model that can answer it**, calibrates each one the same way, and averages
the calibrated forecasts into a multi-model ensemble (MME). It then shows the full
set of outputs an operational PyCPT run produces: skill maps for every model and
the ensemble, EOF patterns and CCA modes, calibrated forecasts, and the flexible
forecast.

The forecasts start on **1 June 2023** and cover July-September 2023 to
December-February 2023-24. Everything is at CHIRPS v3.0's native 0.05° grid: the
69,640 pixels that touch Indonesia's 38-province boundary and have data in every
training season. All numbers on this page come from the
[executed notebook](../notebooks/seasonal-mme-2023.ipynb). Hover, tap or use the
arrow keys on any map or chart to read values; maps load when you choose them, and
the maps in a group zoom and pan together.

::: {.callout-note title="The short result"}
- **From a June start there is skill to work with.** The ensemble's cross-validated
  correlation is 0.55, 0.62, 0.58 and 0.50 for the four seasons from JAS to OND,
  then 0.20 and 0.17 for NDJ and DJF.
- **Combining models helps most where the members are good.** The ensemble is above
  CFSv2 alone for JAS to OND (0.55 against 0.49 for JAS) and has the higher
  correlation in 65% to 90% of pixels. For NDJ and DJF it is slightly below CFSv2.
- **The ensemble is close to the best member, not above it.** GEOSS2S is marginally
  higher for JAS and ASO (0.56 and 0.63); the ensemble is highest for SON and OND.
  Which member is best changes with the lead and is only known afterwards.
- **Calibration costs a little early and pays later.** The plain average of the raw
  models scores 0.65 and 0.66 for JAS and ASO, above the calibrated ensemble. From
  OND on the calibrated ensemble is higher (0.50 against 0.36 for OND).
- **Probabilities beat climatology at every lead.** The ensemble's cross-validated
  RPSS is 0.23 to 0.32 for JAS to OND and 0.10 and 0.09 after that.
- **In 2023 the ensemble called the dry season.** It put 92% to 99% of the area in
  the dry category for ASO to OND; 65% to 77% of the area ended there. For JAS it
  was too dry: most of the area ended near normal.
:::

## Why 1 June

The first version of this case used the 1 November 2023 start of the single-model
page. Its targets, December-February to May-July, turned out to be the seasons
where no model has much skill over Indonesia, and the ensemble's correlation was
0.19 at best. Before choosing another date, a scan measured every start month and
lead with the same settings, on a coarser 0.25° grid where a fit takes seconds.

| 1 Jan | 0.12 | 0.07 | -0.02 | 0.00 | 0.11 | 0.17 |
| 1 Feb | 0.15 | 0.01 | 0.12 | 0.27 | 0.39 | 0.44 |
| 1 Mar | 0.08 | 0.22 | 0.35 | 0.40 | 0.49 | 0.44 |

| 1 Jul | 0.63 | 0.58 | 0.49 | 0.20 | 0.19 | 0.15 |

Source: [skill-calendar.csv](../data/seasonal-mme-2023/skill-calendar.csv), written by `research/scripts/skill_calendar_scan.py`.

The pattern follows the **target season**, not the lead: targets between
June-August and October-December score 0.4 to 0.6 from several start months, and
targets between December-February and May-July score about 0.2 or less from any of
them. A 1 June start has four well-predicted seasons in a row and then two weak
ones, so one page shows both. The date was chosen from this table, which uses the
training years only, not from how the 2023 forecast turned out. The 0.05° results
below came out within 0.03 of the June row.

## Which models, and why these

Eleven catalog models were candidates. Before any skill was computed, a script
downloaded each one with PyCPT's own `download_data` for every target and recorded
whether the download worked, every training year held data, the 2023 forecast held
data, and the **returned target months were the ones requested**.

| Model | JAS | ASO | SON | OND | NDJ | DJF | In the ensemble |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CFSv2 | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| GEOSS2S | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| CanSIPSIC3 | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| CCSM4 | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| CESM1 | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| SPEAR | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| SEAS51c | ok | ok | ok | no such lead | no such lead | no such lead | leads 1 to 3 |
| GCFS2p1 | 1992, 2020 missing | same | same | no such lead | no such lead | no such lead | no |
| SPSv3p5 | 5 years missing | same | same | no such lead | no such lead | no such lead | no |
| METEOFRANCE9 | 1992 missing, no 2023 forecast | same | same | no such lead | no such lead | no such lead | no |
| CanSIPSIC4 | no 2023 forecast | same | same | same | same | same | no |

: Availability for a 1 June 2023 issue with training target years 1992-2020, measured on 16 November 2026. Source: [availability.json](../data/seasonal-mme-2023/availability.json), written by `research/scripts/check_lead_mme_availability.py`.

Two points shaped the design:

- **Training uses target years 1992-2020 (29 years) for every model**, so all
  members and the ensemble share one sample. The period was fixed in the first
  availability check, for the 1 November start, where SPEAR could not supply
  target year 1991. All seven models have every one of these years from 1 June
  too, as the table shows. The single-model case used 1991-2020.
- **SEAS51c forecasts six months**, so from 1 June it ends in November. It joins
  the first three seasons only. The ensemble has **seven members at leads 1 to 3
  and six at leads 4 to 6**.

::: {.callout-warning title="A lead beyond a model's range does not always fail"}
For three-month targets, asking for a season beyond a model's range fails with an
error, as it did here for SEAS51c at leads 4 to 6. Single months behave
differently. In the check for the monthly case, asking PyCPT for SEAS51c's May
forecast from a 1 November start returned a file without an error; its own dates
said 1-30 April, and its values were April's multiplied by 31/30. The fit script
therefore compares the returned target dates with the request for every model and
lead before fitting.
:::

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof timelineLead = selectControl("Highlight", leadChoices, "1")
issueTargets(mme, timelineLead)
```
:::

## One calibration, 78 times

Each model is calibrated at each lead with **CCA** (3 predictor and 3 predictand
EOFs, 2 CCA modes) and **PCR** (3 predictor EOFs), cross-validation window 5, the
settings of the single-model case. Each fit is one call of PyCPT's
`evaluate_models`: 78 fits in all. At 0.05° a fit took 11 to 40 minutes (median 35)
with many running side by side.

The observations are CHIRPS v3.0 three-month totals built from dekads. A pixel is
kept if any part of it touches a province of the supplied 38-province boundary, so
coastal pixels and small islands are included, and if it has data in all 29
training seasons: 69,640 pixels.

The ensemble is PyCPT's `construct_mme`: the **equal-weight average** of the
members' calibrated forecasts, taken separately for the deterministic forecast, the
prediction error variance and the three category probabilities. The notebook
confirms it: the ensemble forecast equals the mean of its members exactly, and
CPT's Pearson map equals the correlation recomputed from the cross-validated
hindcasts to within 0.0001.

## Skill of every member, and of the ensemble

Area-weighted means over Indonesia, cross-validated over 1992-2020. **Pearson
correlation** is 0 for no linear relationship. **2AFC** is the chance that the
hindcasts rank two different years in the observed order, 50% for no skill
[(Mason and Weigel 2009)](https://doi.org/10.1175/2008MWR2553.1).

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof chartMethod = selectControl("Calibration", ["CCA", "PCR"], "CCA")
viewof chartMetric = selectControl("Score", [["Pearson", "Pearson correlation"], ["2AFC (%)", "2AFC"], ["CV RPSS", "Cross-validated RPSS"]], "Pearson")
mmeSkillByLead(mme, chartMethod, chartMetric)
```
:::

| Lead | Target | Members | MME | CFSv2 alone | Best member | Raw multi-model mean | Pixels where MME beats CFSv2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | JAS 2023 | 7 | 0.55 | 0.49 | GEOSS2S, 0.56 | 0.65 | 90% |
| 2 | ASO 2023 | 7 | 0.62 | 0.59 | GEOSS2S, 0.63 | 0.66 | 71% |
| 3 | SON 2023 | 7 | 0.58 | 0.52 | GEOSS2S, 0.55 | 0.56 | 88% |
| 4 | OND 2023 | 6 | 0.50 | 0.48 | CFSv2, 0.48 | 0.36 | 65% |
| 5 | NDJ 2023-24 | 6 | 0.20 | 0.24 | CFSv2, 0.24 | 0.14 | 35% |
| 6 | DJF 2023-24 | 6 | 0.17 | 0.18 | CanSIPSIC3, 0.21 | 0.06 | 45% |

: Pearson correlation of the CCA calibrations, area-weighted mean over 69,640 pixels, cross-validated 1992-2020. Source: [mme-against-members.csv](../data/seasonal-mme-2023/mme-against-members.csv).

Read across a row. For JAS and ASO the ensemble is second of eight, just behind
GEOSS2S. For SON and OND it is above every member. For NDJ it is fourth of seven,
and for DJF third of seven: when the members themselves are weak, their average is
only middling. With PCR the ensemble is almost the same (0.54, 0.62, 0.57, 0.48,
0.22, 0.16).

The raw column deserves a look. Averaging the models' **raw** rainfall, with no
calibration, correlates with the observations at 0.65 and 0.66 for JAS and ASO,
above the calibrated ensemble. Calibration through three EOFs loses a little of the
models' signal at the first two leads and adds to it from OND on, where the raw
average falls to 0.36, 0.14 and 0.06. The raw average is not a forecast product in
any case: it has model biases and no probabilities.

### Probabilities, cross-validated

PyCPT's own probabilistic scores are computed from in-sample probabilities; its
source code calls them "unrealistically optimistic". The notebook builds
cross-validated tercile probabilities instead. For each training year it leaves out
that year and its two neighbours on each side, takes the tercile boundaries and the
error spread from the remaining years, and centres a Student's t distribution on
the left-out year's cross-validated hindcast. The ranked probability skill score
(**RPSS**) compares those probabilities with a climatological forecast built the
same way; above 0 means the model adds information. This construction is this
tutorial's, not CPT's.

| Lead | Target | MME | CFSv2 alone | Highest member |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | JAS 2023 | 0.26 | 0.21 | GEOSS2S, 0.26 |
| 2 | ASO 2023 | 0.32 | 0.31 | GEOSS2S, 0.34 |
| 3 | SON 2023 | 0.28 | 0.23 | GEOSS2S, 0.26 |
| 4 | OND 2023 | 0.23 | 0.22 | CFSv2, 0.22 |
| 5 | NDJ 2023-24 | 0.10 | 0.10 | CanSIPSIC3, 0.10 |
| 6 | DJF 2023-24 | 0.09 | 0.09 | CanSIPSIC3, 0.10 |

: Cross-validated RPSS of the CCA calibrations against a climatological forecast put through the same steps, area-weighted mean, 1992-2020. Source: [skill-by-lead.csv](../data/seasonal-mme-2023/skill-by-lead.csv).

By this score the ensemble is first or second among the calibrated forecasts at
every lead. For JAS to OND its probabilities are about a quarter to a third better
than climatology's by this measure; for NDJ and DJF about a tenth.

### Why a correlation near zero is not "no skill" here

Cross-validation biases correlation downward. A forecast with **no model at all**,
the mean of the other years, correlates *negatively* with the observations: leaving
a wet year out lowers the mean of the rest. The notebook measures it: the no-model
forecast has an area-mean correlation of -0.24 to -0.42 at these six leads
[(Barnston and van den Dool 1993)](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0442(1993)006%3C0963:ADICVS%3E2.0.CO;2).

So 0 is not the no-skill level of a cross-validated correlation, and the 0.17 to
0.20 at the last two leads is not as close to "nothing" as it looks. A calibrated
model's correlation is not simply shifted by that amount either, which is why this
page compares correlations with each other, and reads them alongside the RPSS,
whose reference is that same no-model forecast. The raw-model correlations involve
no fitting and are not affected.

### Where the skill is

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof mapModel = selectControl("Model", modelChoices, "MME")
viewof mapMethod = selectControl("Calibration", [["CCA", "CCA"], ["PCR", "PCR"], ["raw", "None (raw model)"]], "CCA")
viewof mapMetric = selectControl("Score", [["pearson", "Pearson correlation"], ["rpss", "Cross-validated RPSS"]], "pearson")
mmeSkillMaps(mme, geo, mapModel, mapMethod, mapMetric)
```
:::

## EOF patterns and CCA modes

CCA does not relate the two fields pixel by pixel. It first reduces each to a few
**EOFs**, patterns that explain the most year-to-year variance, each with a score
per year. It then finds pairs of combinations of those, the **CCA modes**, whose
score series are as correlated as possible. These views show what each calibration
is built from.

Choose a model, a lead and a mode. The top map is the pattern in the model's
rainfall over the predictor box, the second the pattern in observed rainfall over
Indonesia, and the chart their scores in each training year.

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof patModel = selectControl("Model", memberChoices, "CFSv2")
viewof patLead = selectControl("Lead", leadChoices, "1")
viewof patKind = selectControl("Show", [["cca", "CCA mode"], ["eof", "EOF"]], "cca")
viewof patMode = selectControl("Mode", [["1", "1"], ["2", "2"], ["3", "3 (EOF only)"]], "1")
mmePatterns(mme, geo, patLead, patModel, patKind, patMode)
```
:::

How to read them, and how not to:

- The patterns come from the fit to **all 29 training years**, not from the
  cross-validation folds. A canonical correlation of 0.80 to 0.91 for the first
  JAS mode describes how well the fitted pair matches in-sample. The
  cross-validated correlation of the forecasts it produces is 0.43 to 0.57.
- The predictand EOFs depend on the observations alone, so they are identical for
  every model at a given lead (the notebook checks this). For JAS the first three
  explain 56.0%, 10.7% and 6.4% of the variance: the calibration can describe
  about three quarters of the year-to-year variance of rainfall at 0.05°, and
  one pattern carries most of it.
- Loadings are in CPT's units and are scaled here so each map's largest absolute
  value is 1. Sign and shape carry meaning; magnitude does not.

## The forecasts, model by model

Each calibrated member gives a deterministic total and three tercile probabilities
at every pixel; the ensemble averages them. The first view is PyCPT's standard
probabilistic map: the colour is the most likely category, darker where its
probability is higher. Others show the total, and the anomaly against the
1992-2020 mean of the same season.

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof fcModel = selectControl("Model", modelChoices, "MME")
viewof fcMethod = selectControl("Calibration", ["CCA", "PCR"], "CCA")
viewof fcView = selectControl("Show", [["probability", "Most likely category and probability"], ["anomaly", "Forecast anomaly (mm)"], ["percent", "Forecast as % of normal"], ["total", "Forecast total"], ["observedCategory", "Observed category"], ["observedAnomaly", "Observed anomaly (mm)"], ["observed", "Observed total"]], "probability")
mmeForecastMaps(mme, geo, fcModel, fcMethod, fcView)
```
:::

### Against what happened

Each lead's target is checked against the observed total. The **hit rate** is the
share of area where the most likely category was the one observed; the grey
squares show what always forecasting the most widespread category would have
scored, a reference chosen with hindsight.

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof scoreMethod = selectControl("Calibration", ["CCA", "PCR"], "CCA")
viewof scoreMetric = selectControl("Score", [["hit", "Hit rate"], ["rpss", "RPSS"], ["rmse", "RMSE"]], "hit")
mmeScoresByLead(mme, scoreMethod, scoreMetric)
```
:::

| Lead | Target | Observed below / near / above (% of area) | MME forecast below / above (% of area) | MME hit rate | Reference hit rate | MME RPSS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | JAS 2023 | 23 / 57 / 20 | 80 / 11 | 35% | 57% (near) | 0.03 |
| 2 | ASO 2023 | 65 / 27 / 9 | 92 / 5 | 70% | 65% (below) | 0.40 |
| 3 | SON 2023 | 74 / 23 / 2 | 99 / 0 | 74% | 74% (below) | 0.54 |
| 4 | OND 2023 | 77 / 18 / 6 | 97 / 2 | 78% | 77% (below) | 0.53 |
| 5 | NDJ 2023-24 | 50 / 29 / 21 | 86 / 11 | 55% | 50% (below) | 0.26 |
| 6 | DJF 2023-24 | 36 / 32 / 32 | 75 / 21 | 50% | 36% (below) | 0.16 |

: The CCA ensemble against each target's observation, area-weighted over 69,640 pixels. RPSS here is against 33/34/33% odds, for one outcome per lead. Sources: [issued-2023-06-forecasts.csv](../data/seasonal-mme-2023/issued-2023-06-forecasts.csv), [issued-2023-06-observed.csv](../data/seasonal-mme-2023/issued-2023-06-observed.csv).

The ensemble put most of Indonesia in the dry category at every lead. From ASO to
OND that was what happened: 65% to 77% of the area ended below normal, the
ensemble's hit rate matched or beat the hindsight reference, and its RPSS was 0.40
to 0.54. For JAS it was too dry too early: 57% of the area ended near normal and
the hit rate was 35%. For NDJ and DJF it stayed dry while the observed categories
spread out, yet still scored above the reference. One outcome per lead describes
2023; it is not a measure of skill.

## The flexible forecast: probability of exceedance

A tercile map answers one question. The **flexible forecast** answers others: the
probability that the season total exceeds a chosen amount at each pixel. PyCPT's
`construct_flex_fcst` builds it from the ensemble's deterministic forecast and its
prediction error variance, as a Student's t distribution
([chapter 5](../learn/05-probabilistic-forecasts.ipynb) compares its conventions
with CPT's native ones).

The default threshold is each pixel's **climatological median**, so the map reads
as "chance of a wetter than median season" and 50% means no information. Choose
another percentile to ask about dry or wet extremes. **Click any pixel** to draw
its curves: the forecast distribution against the climatology, as probability of
exceedance and as density, with the observed total marked.

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof flexLead = selectControl("Lead", leadChoices, "1")
viewof flexPercentile = selectControl("Threshold", [["10", "10th percentile (very dry)"], ["20", "20th percentile"], ["33", "33rd percentile"], ["50", "Median"], ["67", "67th percentile"], ["80", "80th percentile"], ["90", "90th percentile (very wet)"]], "50")
mmeFlexible(mme, geo, flexLead, flexPercentile)
```
:::

| Lead | Target | Mean chance of exceeding the median | Area with chance above 50% | Area observed above the median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | JAS 2023 | 35% | 13% | 42% |
| 2 | ASO 2023 | 29% | 6% | 16% |
| 3 | SON 2023 | 22% | 0% | 7% |
| 4 | OND 2023 | 24% | 2% | 11% |
| 5 | NDJ 2023-24 | 33% | 13% | 33% |
| 6 | DJF 2023-24 | 38% | 23% | 46% |

: The CCA ensemble's flexible forecast, area-weighted. Source: [flexible-forecast.csv](../data/seasonal-mme-2023/flexible-forecast.csv).

The curves in the browser are computed from four stored fields per lead (forecast
centre and scale, climatological mean and scale) with the same formula as PyCPT.
The notebook confirms that those fields reproduce PyCPT's own exceedance
probabilities exactly (largest difference 0.0 percentage points). The fitted
climatology is a normal distribution, as in PyCPT's own flexible-forecast figure;
the green dots are the percentiles of the 29 observed totals, which show where
that normal curve fits the data and where it does not.

Like the tercile probabilities, these assume the t distribution describes the
forecast error well. The cross-validated RPSS above is this page's only test of
that. Where a pixel's forecast curve is as wide as its climatology curve, or wider,
the forecast is saying little more than climatology there.

## What this case shows, and what it does not

This is one issue date, seven models, one set of fixed settings and one verifying
year per target. It shows that from a 1 June start a multi-model ensemble is a
little better than CFSv2 alone for the four seasons with skill, close to its best
member without beating it, and no better than CFSv2 for the two weak seasons. It
does not show how other settings behave; the start-month table above is a coarser
0.25° scan. The settings (3 EOFs, 2 CCA modes) were fixed before any skill was
computed and were not tuned per model.

::: {.callout-tip title="This page is a template"}
The [monthly ensemble](monthly-mme-2023.qmd) shows the same outputs for the single
months July to December from the same start, and the subseasonal ensembles
([dekad](dekad-mme-2023.qmd), [weekly](week-mme-2023.qmd), [pentad](pentad-mme-2023.qmd))
show them for five subseasonal models. The [single-model seasonal page](seasonal-leads-2023.qmd),
issued 1 November 2023, is kept as it was until this layout is settled.
:::
